title: Moving to Barcelona With a Dog or Cat: Vet Rules and Costs
description: Rules for bringing a dog or cat to Spain in 2026, what vets in Barcelona charge, and how to find an English-speaking vet.
excerpt: Microchip, rabies shot, paperwork and a local vet: what you need to bring a pet to Barcelona and what routine care costs.
tldr: To bring a dog or cat to Spain in 2026 the animal needs an ISO microchip fitted before a rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel, plus the right health certificate or EU passport. Routine vet visits in Spain typically cost roughly €25 to €40, and vet care is entirely private.

segments.text: Moving to Barcelona with a pet is very doable, and the city is full of dog owners. The paperwork depends on where you are travelling from, so this guide covers the general rules that apply in 2026 and points to the official sources for the details.

content.text: What do I need to bring a dog or cat to Spain in 2026?

segments.text: The core requirement is an ISO-compliant microchip implanted before a rabies vaccination, with that vaccination given at least 21 days before you travel. The microchip must come first, or the vaccination will not count for travel. The animal must also carry the correct document for your country.

items: EU residents travelling within the EU: a European pet passport with the rabies vaccination recorded.
UK residents: an Animal Health Certificate, as UK-issued pet passports are no longer valid for entry into Spain.
Other non-EU countries: an official health certificate endorsed by the exporting country's authority, issued shortly before travel, sometimes with a rabies blood test depending on the country.
Age: dogs, cats and ferrets under 15 weeks old cannot enter Spain, because the minimum age for the rabies vaccine is 12 weeks plus the 21-day wait.
Numbers: no more than five animals travelling together on a non-commercial move.

segments.text: Rules and country lists change, so check the Spanish Ministry of Agriculture (MAPA) page and your own vet before you travel.

content.text: Do I have to register my dog in Barcelona?

segments.text: Yes. Spanish dogs must be microchipped and registered, and once you live in Barcelona you register your animal with the local authority and update the microchip database with your details. Rules vary between regions, so ask the city council or your vet to confirm what applies in Catalonia at the time you arrive.

content.text: Do dog owners need insurance in Spain?

segments.text: Spain's Animal Welfare Law requires civil liability insurance for dog owners, along with a free online training course, leashes in urban areas and cleaning up after your dog. Certain breeds are classed as potentially dangerous and need a special licence and higher insurance cover, in some cases of at least €120,000. Check whether your dog's breed is on the list before you move.

content.text: How much does a vet cost in Barcelona?

segments.text: Vet care in Spain is entirely private. A routine consultation typically costs about €25 to €40, microchipping roughly €30 to €70, and emergency or overnight hospital care in a city can be far higher, sometimes exceeding €300. Vaccinations, sterilisation and dental work are charged separately, so ask for a written estimate.

items: Emergency or overnight hospital stay: can exceed €300.
Vaccinations, sterilisation and dental work: charged per procedure, so get a quote.

segments.text: Prices vary by clinic, and the ranges above come from published guides, not from any particular vet.

content.text: How do I find an English-speaking vet in Barcelona?

segments.text: Ask whether the vet, not only the reception team, can explain diagnoses and consent forms in English, particularly for surgery or emergencies. Some clinics list their languages on their website, and some vets make home visits.

content.text: Can I rent a flat with a pet in Barcelona?

segments.text: It can be harder. Not all landlords accept animals, and Spanish rental contracts often include explicit pet clauses, sometimes with an extra deposit or references. Ask about pets before you view, and get any agreement in writing. Our guide to

content.text: What should I do in the first weeks after arriving?

segments.text: Register with a local vet soon after you arrive, before you need one urgently. Bring your pet's passport or certificate and vaccination record so the vet can set up a file and tell you when the next vaccinations are due. Update the microchip database with your Barcelona address and phone number, and note the nearest 24-hour emergency clinic so you are not searching for one at night.

content.text: Are there rules for dogs in public spaces in Barcelona?

segments.text: Dogs must generally be kept on a lead in streets and public spaces, except in designated off-lead areas, and owners must pick up waste. Local rules on beaches, parks and public transport change, so check the current city council guidance and any signs where you walk. Fines apply for breaches, and the details vary between municipalities.

content.text: What about summer heat and travelling with a pet?

segments.text: Barcelona summers are hot, so walk dogs early or late, avoid hot pavement and never leave a pet in a parked car. If you plan to fly or take a ferry, ask the operator about pet policies well in advance, as many limit the number and size of animals allowed.
This guide is general information, not veterinary or legal advice. Check the current rules with the authorities and a qualified vet.

faqs.q: What do I need to bring a dog to Spain?
faqs.a: An ISO microchip fitted before a rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel, plus an EU pet passport or the correct health certificate for your country.

faqs.q: How much does a vet cost in Spain?
faqs.a: A routine consultation typically costs about €25 to €40, and microchipping around €30 to €70. Emergency hospital care in a city can exceed €300.

faqs.q: Is dog insurance compulsory in Spain?
faqs.a: Civil liability insurance for dog owners is required under Spain's Animal Welfare Law, and potentially dangerous breeds need a licence and higher cover.

faqs.q: Is vet care in Spain public or private?
faqs.a: Private. There is no public veterinary health service, so you pay the vet directly.

faqs.q: Can I find an English-speaking vet in Barcelona?
faqs.a: Yes. Some clinics and home-visit vets work in English. Confirm that the vet can explain diagnoses and consent in English, and browse our Barcelona vet directory.
